extracted.intended_audience: atheists, skeptics, and general readers interested in religion and natural theology
extracted.subtask_description: A religious/philosophical essay arguing that the anatomical structure, placement, limits, and operations of the five external senses (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch) and the union of soul and body provide evidence of a wise, good Creator rather than chance or brute matter. Uses anatomical observation, simple experiments, and thought-experiments aimed at convincing unbelievers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument of Smelling: anatomical placement and mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The instruments of smelling are placed at the top of the nostrils (in the 'sieve-like' or spongy bone) where olfactory nerves pass through holes to a papillous membrane; smelling requires inhalation so that olfactory particles in air strike the papillous tegument to produce smell (demonstrable by holding the breath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page cites the sieve-like bone, papillary membrane, and the simple experiment that holding one's breath prevents being affected by an odor brought under the nose; notes that a learned author had denied this but that experiment refutes the denial. Use of this anatomical/mechanical description and simple experiment is presented as empirical evidence of design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphology of nostrils fits function
rubrics_metrics.description: Nostrils are broader at the bottom to receive more olfactory particles and narrower at the top so that compression of particles more powerfully affects the olfactory membrane and nerves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author treats the shape of the nostrils as a feature adapted to the purpose of smelling — an instance of form following function that supports a design inference. This is used as an example of how structure suits function rather than being accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and smell provide preparatory knowledge of food quality and pleasurable inducement to eat
rubrics_metrics.description: Smell and taste inform us of the good or bad qualities of meat and drink and the pleasure they produce induces us to undertake the daily labour of eating and drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The beneficial role of these senses in survival and habit-formation (pleasure as inducement) is presented as part of the case for wise design; absence of such guidance would render eating more hazardous or less likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch (feeling) is seated in the skin and mediated by papillae
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of feeling (touch) is distributed throughout the skin; microscopes show the skin contains papillae (pyramidal protuberances arising from nerves and associated glands) which are the instruments of feeling, enabling detection of roughness, smoothness, solidity, fluidity, and pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Malpighi, Bobovius, Bergerus and microscope observations: papillae spring from nerves, skin glands opening externally, sweat passages, and the raised skin surface to increase sensitivity. These anatomical observations are treated as empirical proof of specialized sensory instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density and distribution of papillae correlate with tactile acuity (palms, fingertips, tongue, lips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas used extensively for exploration and sensation (palms, fingertips, tip of the tongue, lips) have a larger collection and greater size of papillae and accordingly finer sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This correlation between tissue structure and function (higher papillae density where more sensitive) is used as direct evidence that the sensory apparatus is optimally arranged for its tasks, strengthening the design inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of sensory organs where relevant media pass (air, light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments of smelling are located in the path of air used in respiration; the eye is adapted to receive light; the ear to receive sounds carried through air; sensory organs are placed 'just where' the relevant medium continually passes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author emphasizes location as purposeful: senses are 'found exactly in the place through which the Air continually passes' (for smell) or otherwise where the pertinent physical medium interacts with the organ. This is a criterion for judging whether an organ is well-designed for its task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different sensory modalities are adapted to different physical properties (light vs sound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sight is adapted to light rays (moving in straight lines) to observe visible objects and their colors; hearing conveys motion and percussion and transmits through curvatures rather than straight rays, enabling detection of things hidden from sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction of modality-specific adaptation supports the argument that different kinds of external motion require different sensory instruments; the author uses this to show complementary roles of the senses and the sophistication of the arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to artificial instruments: organized function implies a designer
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as artificial machines (watches, mills, houses) show a maker because they are formed for an end, so the complex and purposive structure of the senses implies a Maker with understanding and ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument by analogy is explicit: the author invites readers to compare bodily instruments to crafted machines, arguing that one would credit the artisan with purpose — thus one should credit a Creator for bodily contrivances. This is presented as a standard method of inference from function/structure to agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical demonstration and everyday experience as epistemic basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated experiments and daily experience (e.g., holding breath to test smell, microscopic observation of papillae, observing loss of senses leading to misery) provide certain knowledge about how senses operate even if the ultimate causes are unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses experiments and lived experience as sufficient to compel the inference of design: the sensory facts are observable and repeatedly confirmed, which the author treats as a reliable ground for concluding a wise Creator rather than chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness/limits of the senses are intentional and beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: The very limits of our senses (their being neither too acute nor too blunt) are argued to contribute to happiness — e.g., if eyes were microscopic we would see repulsive swarms; if telescopic we would be obstructed by vapors; if smell as acute as hunting-dogs we would be constantly overwhelmed; hyper-acute tastes, hearing, or touch would be unpleasant or disabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author uses thought-experiments and testimony about instruments (microscopes/telescopes/long tubes) to argue that limitations prevent sensory overload and allow appropriate focus. Limits themselves count as evidence of wise design rather than a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of sensory faculties among people is not random and argues against chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people are born with the senses in the same arrangement; their mutual relations (eye suited to light, ear to sound, tongue to taste, skin to touch) cannot be the product of chance because chance would act indifferently and not produce such orderly, frequent, and constant results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The uniformity and regularity of sensory faculties across humans is treated as probabilistic evidence against chance explanations and in favor of a purposeful Creator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument from the misery of lacking senses or understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: If humans lacked the external senses or understanding, their condition would be miserable (blind, deaf, insensible, brutish); this necessity of senses and reason to human flourishing argues that their provision is an important good and deserving of gratitude to their provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author uses imaginative scenarios (a man with none of the senses, Nebuchadnezzar's loss of understanding) to show the indispensable value of these faculties; absence functions as a negative test for their importance and intentional bestowal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of soul and body is mysterious and resists mechanistic reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner in which an immaterial soul is united to and affected by the body (and vice versa) is profoundly unintelligible; neither matter alone nor known motions can adequately account for understanding, perception, and volitional effects on body — this inscrutability points toward a non-mechanistic cause and implies the need for a Creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that whether one posits corporeal thinking matter or an incorporeal soul, the facts (soul feeling pain when body is burned; will causing bodily movement; localized nerve control) remain inexplicable in purely material terms. The epistemic gap (experience without explanatory mechanism) is used to press the design/theological conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds of soul's operation correspond to anatomical nerve distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul does not operate the whole body at will but only those parts whose nerves arise from the cerebellum and backbone (arms, hands, legs); other organs (heart, stomach, bowels) have different nerve origins and do not obey the soul's will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This anatomical restriction of voluntary action is marshaled as a fact the atheist cannot explain away; it is used to show that the soul-body union is limited and structured, reinforcing the claim of a deliberate ordering rather than random happenstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all bodily parts convey sensation to the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Hair, nails, and bones are insensible; the brain can suffer injury without communicating sensation to the soul; hence the soul's perceptions are selective and mediated, not omnipresent in matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These observations about insensible parts of the body are used to argue that sensation is tied to specialized instruments and cannot be explained by a blanket property of matter — supporting the claim of specialized design and an immaterial element whose operations are localized.
